NodeMaven is the better choice for anyone buying proxies, especially for social media, multi-accounting and anti-detect browsers: it supports SOCKS5 (Nimble's proxies are HTTP/HTTPS only), publishes its pool, rolls over traffic and costs $2.20/GB on monthly plans against Nimble's $5.30/GB docs rate. NodeMaven and Nimble both charge more than budget providers, but for very different reasons. NodeMaven charges for IP quality: it screens residential and mobile IPs before assignment so accounts are less likely to be flagged. blocks.text: NodeMaven in 2026: what you get

NodeMaven competes on IP quality rather than pool size. Every residential and mobile IP passes through its IP Quality Filter before it is assigned, with three strictness levels, and the company reports a 95% clean-IP rate. Proxyway's testing found the filter lowered fraud scores noticeably on sticky sessions. The pool is 30M+ residential plus 250K mobile IPs in 150+ countries, traffic rolls over, and you get up to 10% cashback on used gigabytes plus a guarantee that pays out for bad proxies.

Strengths: IP Quality Filter screens IPs before you get them; Long sticky sessions for account work; Traffic rollover and cashback; Quality guarantee that pays for bad IPs. Weak spots: Smaller pool than mass-market networks; No datacenter proxies; Pay-as-you-go rate is double the plan rate.
Nimble in 2026: what you get

Nimble (Nimbleway) is an AI-first web-data platform. It offers residential proxies with fast response times and unlimited concurrency, but most of its product investment goes into the Nimble Browser, SERP and e-commerce APIs, and data-services plans that start in the thousands of dollars per month. It does not disclose its residential pool size, and its per-GB rates are among the highest here, so it competes on finished results rather than cheap traffic.

Strengths: Strong managed APIs and an AI-driven browser; Unlimited concurrency on proxies; Credits shared across all Nimble products; Free 5,000-page API trial. Weak spots: No published pool size; HTTP/HTTPS only, no SOCKS5 on proxies; High per-GB price for raw residential traffic.
Pricing: NodeMaven vs Nimble

NodeMaven charges $4.50/GB pay-as-you-go and $2.20/GB on monthly plans, with residential and mobile traffic on one balance. A $3.50 trial includes 750 MB. Unused traffic rolls over, and you earn up to 10% cashback on used traffic. ISP proxies start at $2.99 per IP with unlimited traffic.

Nimble's plan cards list residential proxy traffic at $8/GB pay-as-you-go, falling through credit packages ($150 and $600 entry packages) toward $5.30/GB; its current developer documentation lists $5.30/GB for residential traffic without a commitment. Annual billing saves 15%. Its scraping APIs bill $0.90 to $1.45 per 1,000 URLs depending on rendering.

At 10 GB a month, NodeMaven is the cheaper option at about $45 against $53 for Nimble, roughly 15% less. Buying 100 GB, you would pay about $220 with NodeMaven and $530 with Nimble: a 58% saving in NodeMaven's favour. The sticker price is only half of it. NodeMaven's unused traffic carries forward, while Nimble's does not (credits usable across nimble products), so if your usage swings from month to month NodeMaven can work out cheaper than the per-GB numbers suggest.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

Nimble does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. NodeMaven lists '30M+ residential + 250K mobile' and Nimble lists 'Not published'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, NodeMaven lists 150+ countries and Nimble lists Worldwide. On targeting, NodeMaven offers country, region, city and ISP, while Nimble offers country, state and city.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Protocol support is a real difference here. NodeMaven supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5, while Nimble offers HTTP, HTTPS. If your tooling needs SOCKS5, for example some anti-detect browsers, desktop apps or non-HTTP traffic, that settles it in NodeMaven's favour. On sessions, NodeMaven offers rotating or long sticky sessions (multi-day), and Nimble offers auto-rotation by default; sticky sessions available. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: Nimble wins. The deciding factor for Nimble: its managed APIs remove much of the anti-bot work. The limitation on the NodeMaven side: the quality filter matters less for high-rotation crawling.

SERP and rank tracking: Nimble. Nimble has the edge here. Why: its SERP API and search agents return structured results. How NodeMaven compares: workable, but you pay a premium for filtering you may not need.

Social media and multi-account management: NodeMaven. NodeMaven has the edge here. Why: pre-screened, low-fraud-score IPs with long sticky sessions. How Nimble compares: no SOCKS5 and a high per-GB cost make it a poor fit for account work.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Nimble. Nimble has the edge here. Why: dedicated e-commerce data APIs. How NodeMaven compares: fine for light checks.

Ad verification and geo-testing: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With NodeMaven: good quality but a smaller pool. With Nimble: good geo targeting but no published pool data. Run the same small test on both before committing.
Tight budgets: NodeMaven. NodeMaven has the edge here. Why: mid-priced on plans, expensive on PAYG. How Nimble compares: per-GB rates are among the highest here.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. NodeMaven: $3.50 trial with 750 MB. Nimble: Free trial of 5,000 web pages on its APIs. Verification and payment rules differ too. NodeMaven: Standard. Nimble: Sales-led onboarding for data-services plans. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test NodeMaven and Nimble before you commit
The quickest way to choose between NodeMaven and Nimble is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (NodeMaven: $3.50 trial with 750 MB; Nimble: free trial of 5,000 web pages on its APIs).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, NodeMaven comes out ahead in 2, Nimble in 3, and 1 is a tie. That makes Nimble the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: NodeMaven is strongest for social media and multi-account management, while Nimble is strongest for teams that want structured data rather than raw IPs. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
